record.title: A code-generation study reports that structural compliance can conceal incorrect answers
record.summary: Adikari and Herath evaluated three cost-efficient models across eight combinations of model, coding-agent tool and prompt format on 992 Project Euler problems converted to Java Spring Boot methods. They report near-ceiling compliance with required method signatures and 7,936 executed requests, but only 12.9% of returned answers were correct; 38.4% of generated methods did not compute the value they returned. This is a single-generation, author-reported evaluation on a narrow algorithmic corpus, not a measured rate for enterprise code or deployed assistants.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that generated Java methods met the mandated signature while 38.4% of methods did not compute the value they returned, and only 12.9% of returned answers were correct in this evaluation.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The reported results come from three cost-efficient models, four model/coding-tool pairings and two prompt layouts on 992 Project Euler problems in a one-shot Java Spring Boot generation regime.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report an inverse association between their semantic-compliance and correctness measures, but explicitly caution that denominators differ and that the correlation does not establish that attempting more causes lower accuracy.

evidence_gaps.description: The study's method classification, generated code counts and correctness results have not been independently reproduced; no author code artifact was located in this review.
Whether the measured structure/function gap occurs in repository-level, enterprise or iterative code-generation tasks is unknown; the current evaluation uses one-shot Project Euler-to-Spring methods.

brief.importance_rationale: If reproduced, the study's bounded result would materially affect how code-generation benchmarks distinguish valid structure from actual computation: correct signatures and high response rates can coexist with many answers that are fabricated or wrong. This is notable for evaluation design, but its single-shot Project Euler setup does not establish failure rates in deployed or enterprise coding work.
limitations: The experiment uses Project Euler numeric problems represented as Java Spring Boot methods; it does not measure enterprise application development, repository-level tasks or deployed coding-assistant failure rates.
Each task/configuration received one generation, so the reported proportions do not estimate variability across sampling runs or establish a stable model failure probability.
The corpus likely has contamination exposure: the authors note early Project Euler problems are widely discussed online and report that many literal matches cluster in the early range.
The paper reports partial generated-code coverage across configurations, varying from 80.1% to 100.0% in Table II; missing methods and runtime errors affect denominators.

The reported negative correlations do not establish that better semantic compliance causes lower accuracy. The paper explains that denominators and task difficulty differ; GPT-5.4 mini's strongest conditional correctness point is concentrated among easier early problem identifiers.

The paper's classification is syntactic/static and its harness only covers specified output patterns; complex semantics, human review, iterative repair, repository context and adversarially stronger test suites are not evaluated.
All results are author-reported; the research desk did not inspect raw generated artifacts, run the public/author code or independently reproduce the evaluation.
brief.summary: Adikari and Herath evaluated three cost-efficient models across eight combinations of model, coding-agent tool and prompt format on 992 Project Euler problems converted to Java Spring Boot methods. They report near-ceiling compliance with required method signatures and 7,936 executed requests, but only 12.9% of returned answers were correct; 38.4% of generated methods did not compute the value they returned. This is a single-generation, author-reported evaluation on a narrow algorithmic corpus, not a measured rate for enterprise code or deployed assistants.

technical.claimed_result: Across 7,593 methods, the authors report that all methods had the required method signature, while 2,913 (38.4%) did not compute the value returned. Across 7,936 runtime requests, 6,981 returned an answer and 898 were correct (12.9% of returned answers). They also report a 19.3% correctness rate among answers from genuine computation attempts. These are author-reported outcomes from the stated models, tools, prompts and Project Euler task corpus.
technical.compute_or_cost: No matched inference-cost or total-compute comparison was established in the inspected paper. It reports per-request service timing but does not provide a full economic comparison or general cost-per-correct-result frontier.
technical.demonstrated_result: The primary manuscript specifies an eight-configuration evaluation, code taxonomy and execution pipeline and reports its tables. the research desk inspected the paper but did not reproduce its generation, static-analysis or runtime results.
technical.implementation_status: Accepted manuscript for the 2026 International Conference on Advanced Computing Technologies (ICACT); the final version of record is expected on IEEE Xplore. No public code artifact was linked from the inspected arXiv record.
technical.mechanism: The authors classify each generated method by how it produces an answer, statically checking code structure and shortcut behavior, then execute the same generated methods against Project Euler problems so functional results can be conditioned on the production strategy.
technical.novelty: Joins structural/strategy classification and functional execution on the same generated code, enabling the authors to show that emitted form, returned values and actual correctness can diverge under one-shot code generation.
technical.regime: One-shot generation of Java Spring Boot service methods for Project Euler problems 1–1000, with 992 provided and 8 withheld as missing-input probes. Eight configurations combine three cost-efficient models, four model/tool pairings and two prompt layouts; iteration is prohibited and hardcoded answers are explicitly disallowed. Each method is statically classified and endpoints are run once, for 7,936 requests.
technical.reproducibility: The seven-page accepted manuscript and arXiv metadata were inspected. The paper gives its corpus, prompts, models, task classification and server design, but this activation did not locate code/data artifacts or independently reproduce the study. Results are one generation per task/configuration and likely affected by Project Euler corpus exposure.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper crosses Gemini Flash 3 with Cursor, GPT-5.4 mini with Cursor, and Claude Haiku 4.5 with both Cursor and Claude Code; each of these four model/tool pairings is evaluated under two prompt layouts. It compares structure/strategy classification with execution correctness on the same methods; there is no separate human-code or frontier-model control in the inspected study.

brief.title: A code-generation study reports that structural compliance can conceal incorrect answers
brief.why_it_matters: The study evaluates structure and executed function on the same generated code, and reports that a valid signature can coexist with fabricated or incorrect output. If the narrow result generalizes, source-shape checks and answer-rate measures alone can miss severe failure modes in code-generation evaluations. The paper does not establish prevalence outside its specific tasks, models and one-shot setup.
